title: Peace, Shared Songs and My Unpaid Portrait
subtitle: Native cooperative games, shared puzzles and stories for an optional companion

opening.title: The Rehearsal Had Two Controllers and One Unnecessary Throne
paragraphs: I placed two controllers on a velvet cushion beneath the portrait. It was meant to suggest equality. Tank looked at the cushion, then at the only chair facing the screen.
'Where's the other person sit?'
Nigga, equality had arrived ahead of the furniture.

Rae pulled up a second chair. Nia moved the cushion so both controllers could reach their cables. My wife sat in the chair I had reserved for the host and asked whether I planned to stand there explaining the arrangement all night.
'I'm establishing the mood.'
'You've established a queue.'

The final wording waited in its folder. The signing table stood level, the light reached the page and Mika had timed the walk from the buffet without including any pause for my autobiography. We were going to try sharing actual controls before celebrating an agreement about sharing a room.
Dez arrived wearing the disputed jacket. Auntie June followed carrying its empty hanger.
'Evidence,' June told me.
Dez said a hanger could not prove the weather in 1967. June said she had brought it to hang the coat, which was a far more devastating reply than any courtroom flourish I could have supplied.

Both veterans still claimed the other had never signed the old Blue Comet agreement. This one had acquired enough working pens to alarm a stationery wholesaler. I had bought the gold one. Nia preferred the plain black one because it actually wrote.
Rae tested both. 'Yours writes too,' she told Nia. 'Just not in a recognised direction.'
Nia smiled. 'You understood the invitation.'
'Eventually.'
They would dance after the signing. Their only unresolved question was whether Rae could persuade Nia that being good at a contract did not require counting every step before the music began.
Kit had her karaoke song ready and her reading glasses attached to a cord. Remy admired the practical innovation, then discovered his crown prevented him from putting on his headphones.

Velvet Payroll removed the crown, set it on the table and told him to preserve his head for the performance. She had been paid, her shoes were fastened and her stage time existed on an actual clock. A powerful woman with excellent grounds for happiness.

Mercedes checked the music. Porsche checked that the photographer understood which pictures people wanted. Nobody needed another staged candid in which Rae pretended not to notice a lens six inches from her coffee.

Dre brought the blue controller and a casserole. He was a Crip with a hot dish, not an available metaphor for my summit title. He wanted a clear space to set the food and the particular colour of plastic he had chosen.
I offered the gold controller. 'Nigga, you keep the expensive-looking problem,' he said.

Darnell appeared behind him with a little case and an offer to sponsor fireworks. Velvet asked whether the sponsorship involved money or cocaine. He said relationships. She told him her actual relationships had already paid for the show.

He tried describing a yacht. The host opened the lift before the description acquired a second deck. Darnell went to find a different audience. Dre stayed to ask Rosa whether the casserole needed warming.
Mika suggested using the model hotel to rehearse the procession. I liked the idea until they assigned my paper figure to hold the door.
'I have a speaking role.'
'You have a useful arm,' Rae said.
Shawna kissed that arm through my sleeve. Suddenly the assignment developed possibilities.

Some games would give two people separate characters. Some would divide their information. Some would give one person a smaller helping role. Others could simply be enjoyed together with one person operating the controls.
June said she might watch. Dez said she might try. Neither statement triggered an emergency meeting.
I looked up at the portrait, whose enormous expression appeared to endorse every arrangement. That was generous of it, considering the evening had still authorised none of its cost.
Then Rae handed Nia a controller and asked which role she wanted. A normal question, asked without a trumpet.
I sat beside Shawna, took the other available chair properly and waited to hear the answer.
The Second Great Butch vs. Stud War had reached the dangerous stage where people might enjoy themselves enough to forget who was supposed to receive credit.

games.case_title: The Hero Had to Wait for His Friends
scene: Secret of Mana's party adventure made me offer to be the summit's central hero. Auntie June asked whether that position involved carrying chairs. I said it involved vision.
'Then carry two,' she replied. 'One for each eye.'
Dez laughed into her tea. June had been telling her what needed moving since the Blue Comet dispute of 1967; the instructions had apparently improved with age.
The original game's companions had to join before shared control became available. Rae liked that the plan required checking the actual party rather than handing out imaginary jobs.
I carried the chairs. Nia tested the second controller with Rae while Tank found the correct cable. Nobody appointed me commander of their buttons.
Dez touched the jacket folded beside her. 'She lent this with a lecture about the pockets.' June said a borrower deserved to know where things went.
Both women accepted the dry chairs I supplied. Nigga, I had achieved a modest diplomatic victory entirely through furniture.
games.pleasure: The original 1993 adventure offers a colourful party journey with native cooperative fighting once companions join. Its overhead view removes free-camera steering, while towns, equipment, magic and connected areas give the journey continuity.
games.burden: Combat runs in real time. Original manual instructions include held dashing and charged attacks, plus Y opening the paused ring menu. Original SNES two-player play needs two controllers; a third needs a multiplayer adapter. Collection of Mana supports up to three. The 2018 remake is excluded.
games.first: Enjoy the solo opening together or use an existing shared save after an ally joins. Try moving, opening the ring and one familiar encounter. The second player should choose their own role rather than automatically receiving every difficult job.
games.ruling: Try the original adventure if its real-time demands and hardware arrangement suit. The appointed hero has discovered that a useful party member sometimes begins by carrying two chairs.

games.case_title: The Ferry Had Room for Another Chair
scene: Spiritfarer's ferry made Mika describe our convention floor as a vessel carrying everyone toward a farewell. Velvet asked whether the vessel had paid its entertainment bill.
'Yes,' I said proudly. She checked her phone. 'It has. Continue floating.'
June wanted a seat near Dez without sitting beneath the speaker. Tank found one. Rosa brought tea and asked whether either wanted anything in it.
The game's caring chores and eventual goodbyes gave the room a quieter subject. Dez remembered replacing the borrowed jacket's worn lining. June remembered choosing the colour.
They disagreed gently about the colour. Neither disputed that someone had kept the coat.
Nia and Rae tried their different roles without pretending they were identical. I offered to supervise their shared voyage. Shawna asked me to carry the empty cups back instead.
On my return, June was showing Dez a photograph. Velvet had sat down to listen. Our vessel had finally stopped announcing every passenger over the public-address system.
games.pleasure: Build and travel on a ferry, care for spirits, gather materials and eventually say goodbye. The Farewell Edition includes the expanded character stories. Native local cooperation pairs Stella with Daffodil, giving two people a shared place to inhabit.
games.burden: Movement includes jumping and gliding; chores, recipes and resources accumulate. The cat's role differs from Stella's. A previously inspected secondary walkthrough identifies Elena's later timed Gold Dragon challenge, so the gentle presentation is not a no-rush guarantee. Bereavement is the central theme.
games.first: Meet a passenger, walk around the boat and try one chore in each role. Check whether both people enjoy what their character can do. Leave the larger building plan alone until the small shared activity feels worthwhile.
games.ruling: Consider the caring ferry journey if its chores, unequal roles and bereavement feel welcome. Our vessel now serves tea without demanding that every passenger deliver a farewell speech.

games.case_title: The Fallen Star Wanted Its Own Billing
scene: Pode's rock and fallen star gave Remy and Velvet an irresistible casting dispute. He wanted to be the star. She asked whether his contract supported that interpretation.
'I'm naturally luminous,' he said. 'You're standing under my lamp,' she replied.
Rae wanted to try the characters' different abilities. Nia chose the other role, then asked what Rae needed from her before either moved.
I declared this an ideal model for the signing. Mika immediately assigned me the heavy end of the table. Nigga, somehow I kept auditioning for light and being cast as rock.
Remy and Velvet settled their quarrel by taking turns, discovering that each preferred doing something different from what they had predicted.
Kit adjusted the real lamp so both could see. She refused to select a winner for the billing dispute.
The beautiful caverns kept their spatial puzzles. Our room solved one of its own when the table stopped blocking a chair.
Shawna admired my effort. I asked whether I glowed. 'A little sweaty,' she said.
games.pleasure: A rock and a fallen star explore Norwegian-inspired caverns, using different abilities to bring an ancient environment to life and solve spatial puzzles. The Switch edition supports one or two players on one system.
games.burden: You still move characters through three-dimensional spaces and coordinate their positions and abilities. The store's cooperative and gentle-looking presentation does not prove no held movement, no tricky jumps or no timed sections throughout. The assigned edition is Switch; PC controller requirements are not imported here.
games.first: Try the first shared room and let each person explain what their character appears able to change. Check movement, positioning and the viewpoint before tackling a long puzzle. Switch roles only if both people would like to.
games.ruling: Try the complementary pair if its movement and spatial coordination suit both players. My rock performance has cleared a chair, and the star may negotiate its own lamp.

games.case_title: The Farm Did Not Recognise My Opening Bell
scene: Stardew Valley made Rosa imagine a small farm with enough room for flowers and no stage. Tank immediately asked what they would grow for dinner.
I offered to fund an agricultural wing of the summit. Rae asked whether it came with a portrait on the barn. My pause answered before I did.
Nia wanted to understand the active day and shared setup before promising an evening of joint farming. Rae agreed. They chose one modest task instead of naming an estate.
June said the Blue Comet had once tried growing herbs behind the kitchen. Dez said June had watered the same plastic basil for a month.
'It stayed green,' June replied.
The game had enough tools, seasons and activities without my bell announcing every crop. Rosa and Tank looked at the starting work together and kept their plans small.
Shawna took the bell from my hand. 'This is why nobody lets you near livestock.'
I told her I possessed pastoral charm. She asked me to demonstrate it by remaining seated.
games.pleasure: Farming, friendships, seasons, crafting and exploration create a place that can grow alongside a group. The current inspected PC listing advertises online cooperation and shared-screen support, allowing genuine joint work rather than only discussion beside one controller.
games.burden: An active day, energy, inventories, travel, fishing and combat create different demands. Multiplayer pause behavior must be checked; a partner does not automatically stop the clock. Many recipes and social schedules can turn leisure into planning. Record the actual installed version before comparing features.
games.first: Plant a small patch or take one walk together. Inspect movement, item selection and what happens to time when a menu opens. Avoid choosing a mining or fishing challenge as the sole measure of whether village life appeals.
games.ruling: Visit the shared farm if its active days and management appeal after checking multiplayer pacing. Our agricultural wing remains a single conversation with no portrait on the barn.

games.case_title: The Peace Palace Had No Back Door
scene: Minecraft's Creative mode encouraged Mika to propose a block-built model of the signing room. I began with a triumphal entrance tall enough to accommodate my reputation.
Rae began with the table. Nia added space around it. Tank asked where a person could leave. I pointed proudly at the triumphal entrance.
'Without walking through your announcement,' he clarified.
June said the Blue Comet had one narrow exit and too many people trying to look unbothered in it. Dez said June had blocked it while arguing about the jukebox.
Mika added another door. The model improved instantly.

The camera and placement still needed an actual trial, and compatible editions mattered before anyone promised a shared build. Meanwhile, our imaginary architecture was already learning from the people who would use it.
I put a tiny portrait above the entrance. Shawna moved it into a side room. 'Private collection,' she said.
Nigga, my first museum had opened without public funding or a compulsory route through it.

games.burden: Moving while steering a three-dimensional view and precisely placing blocks can be substantial work. Creative mode changes survival pressure, not those demands. Official comparison lists controller support for Bedrock, not Java, and split-screen only on consoles; do not plan PC couch split-screen.
games.first: Choose the exact edition and arrange compatible separate-device play if sharing online or locally. In Creative mode, try looking around and placing a few blocks before planning anything large. A wall with one window is an adequate architectural brief.
games.ruling: Build together in a compatible setup if camera movement and placement suit. The model's second door stays open, and its portrait collection may be visited entirely by choice.

games.case_title: The Island Host Misplaced His Mandate
scene: Animal Crossing's island home made me ask what sort of neighbour I would be. Rosa said one who installed a fountain before learning when the bins went out.
I called that civic ambition. Rae called it plumbing with an audience.
Kit wanted a quiet corner to decorate. Remy wanted to visit and bring something ridiculous. They checked which shared mode actually gave them the freedom they expected.
Dez remembered how the old club's jukebox had acquired a handwritten AUNTIE JUNE'S CHOICE sign. June said it was temporary. 'It lasted longer than the curtains,' Dez replied.
Nia wrote the new jukebox sentence plainly: everybody could choose songs, and nobody's name owned the machine.
I asked whether the host received priority. Seven faces turned toward me. Nigga, the island had developed a remarkably efficient weather system.
Shawna suggested I bring a useful gift instead. I offered the gold fountain. She asked for batteries.
I found batteries. My promising career as a neighbour survived its first planning objection.

games.burden: Crafting, tool selection, storage and repeated dialogue can create menu work. Same-system roles and restrictions deserve a practical check before assuming everyone has identical freedom. The page reflects current updates, so check the installed version; this card does not certify every activity as untimed.

games.case_title: The Portal Opened Onto My Own Mistake
scene: Portal 2's cooperative chambers made me and Rae a dangerous combination: she wanted to understand the route, and I wanted to explain it before looking.
'Over there,' I said. 'Where?' 'By the significant wall.'
She turned toward me. 'Nigga, every wall got significance if you walk into it.' Nia laughed so suddenly that her pen rolled under the table.
We stopped to retrieve it. Rae described what she could actually see. I finally looked at my own view and discovered I had been discussing the wrong direction with magnificent confidence.
The first-person aiming and coordinated actions were real things to test. My commentary was an optional obstacle.
Across the room, Remy rehearsed his entrance through one door while Velvet left through another. Mika asked them to exchange places. They managed without inventing interdimensional law.
I gave Rae one clear description. She answered with one useful instruction. Something worked.
Shawna applauded softly. 'A portal to competence,' she said. I resisted announcing that I had designed it.

games.burden: First-person movement, aiming, spatial transformations and coordinating actions remain substantial catches. Steam declares play without timed input, but that declaration is not a tested guarantee that every cooperative manoeuvre avoids urgency or awkward timing. Both camera comfort and joint execution need direct trials.

games.ruling: Try the dedicated cooperative puzzles if first-person aiming and coordination suit both people. The host's directional commentary is now required to identify an actual place before becoming advice.

games.case_title: Two Geese and an Unattended Sash
scene: Untitled Goose Game put two determined troublemakers before us. Velvet and Remy exchanged a look I should have recognised as a warning about my unattended ceremonial sash.
I was explaining how shared mischief required trust when Velvet asked me to inspect a stage light. Remy quietly lifted the sash from my chair.
By the time I returned, it decorated the buffet's bread basket. GRAND CONVENOR OF ROLLS, Kit announced.
Rae laughed hard enough to lean against Nia. Nia caught her elbow and kept laughing too. The summit had found its first completely unanimous resolution.
The geese's real-time trouble still needed a practical control check. Our trouble required only leaving two entertainers bored within reach of fabric.
I went to reclaim my office. Rosa put a fresh roll into my hand and said the basket wore the sash well.
Shawna untied it after everyone had eaten. 'You can have your title back now.'
Nigga, I had been defeated by two performers and temporarily replaced by bread.

games.burden: Stealth, pursuit, object handling and positioning operate in real time. Some tasks require observing routines and acting at a useful moment; held inputs and later time challenges need checking. A charming goose is still capable of making a control scheme demanding.
games.first: Explore the first garden together and try moving, honking and handling one object before attempting an elaborate prank. Agree whether either person wants hints. Enjoy an accidental comic moment without turning every task into a performance target.
games.ruling: Try the comic mischief if pursuit and object handling feel enjoyable. Our ceremonial sash may return to its owner once the bread basket finishes its entirely successful term.

games.case_title: The Ribbon Connected Two Unrelated Plans
scene: Unravel Two's connected Yarnys made Mika suggest a ribbon linking the two ceremonial pens. I approved the symbolism before asking whether anyone planned to move them.
Rae tested one pen. Nia reached for the other. The ribbon caught my champagne flute and brought it halfway across the cloth.
'Beautiful unity,' Rae said. 'Where do you want the spill?'
I blamed insufficient tension. Kit said that was the first inaccurate description of the room all evening.
The game's physical connection could create shared possibilities and coordination demands. Our pens needed to stay ordinary pens. Mika cut the ribbon and tied two small bows instead.
June took one bow and attached it to the jacket Dez had been carrying. Dez pretended to object, then straightened it carefully.
Nia tested the free pen again. Her signature still looked like a bird escaping a saucepan. Rae said she could recognise it now.
Shawna rescued my flute. 'You can connect with me later,' she whispered. 'Without tying anything to the table.'

Its warmth does not establish an easy route through every chase or challenge; check any assistance options in the actual build.

games.case_title: Eighty Days to Find the Correct Coat
scene: 80 Days made June describe the old jacket's supposed travels. According to her, it had visited three cities before Dez remembered that borrowing eventually involved returning.
Dez said June had recommended two of those cities herself. 'Then you kept the coat,' June said. 'Because you said the weather looked terrible.'
I offered to commission a map. Rae asked whether the map would arrive before the jacket already sitting on the chair beside us.
Nia wanted a simple settlement: the coat could be returned, lent again when asked, and kept out of the expense claim for my portrait.
'That last bit wandered in,' I said. 'Like the coat,' Shawna replied.
The game had routes, luggage and schedules to weigh. Our shared discussion needed no extra controller, but it did need me to stop proposing freight insurance for a sixty-year argument.
Dez draped the jacket over June's shoulders to check the fit. June smiled.
Nobody called that surrender. Tank called it time to bring the dessert trolley closer.

games.case_title: The Past Said Blue; the Future Said Burgundy
scene: The Past Within gave June and Dez an immediate reason to dispute separate accounts of the same object. June remembered the jacket as blue. Dez remembered replacing its burgundy lining.
'Those are different parts,' Rae said. Both women paused, irritated by the possibility of a cheap solution.
Nia and Rae tried the game's separate perspectives, checking their own screens before describing what they saw. I hovered between them like an unsolicited weather report.
'Can I provide context?' I asked. 'You can provide a chair,' Nia said.
I brought one and sat in it, which was not quite what she meant. Shawna moved it back far enough that my knees stopped entering Rae's view.
The eerie mystery required communication, copies and devices, not simply two people staring at one display. Our coat mystery required noticing an inside and an outside.
Dez turned the lining out. June touched the blue sleeve. Both accounts survived.
I declared reconciliation. Rae asked me to wait until somebody had finished a sentence before installing the plaque.

games.case_title: Kirby Was Not Available to Clear the Buffet
scene: Kirby and the Forgotten Land made Tank ask whether the pink hero could help with the remaining buffet. Rosa told him the buffet already had sufficient heroic attention.
Remy wanted Kirby. Velvet wanted to know what the second character actually did before accepting a role described vaguely as also there.
Rae checked the different jobs with them. Nia watched the first trial while Mika cleared enough table space for both controllers.
I offered a magnificent introduction for Player Two. Velvet said she preferred actual information. Nigga, my ceremonial skill set was experiencing another small recession.
The game had real platforming, combat and timed challenges beyond its welcoming appearance. Remy liked the movement; Velvet wanted to switch roles once they understood them.
They did. Nothing about the exchange reduced either performer's billing.
Across the room, June took another pastry. Dez quietly moved the napkin closer. Tank observed that partnership could be measured in the distance between food and a clean sleeve.
Rosa kissed his cheek and handed him the empty tray.

games.case_title: The Farm Kept Growing While the Pen Went Around
scene: Farm Together's continuing little tasks made Tank wonder whether a place could carry on without its host supervising every minute. Rae looked at me. Nia looked at me. Shawna spared a glance.
I said I was sensing an unrelated agenda.
Rosa liked the idea of returning to a shared farm for a modest job. She also liked the right to leave it alone when dinner, sleep or other people sounded better.
June passed the signed page to Dez. Dez read the jukebox sentence once more, smiled and added her name. Nia signed beneath the agreed final wording with her magnificent, terrible handwriting.
Rae recognised it anyway.
The game's persistent work could become pleasant or burdensome depending on what people wanted. Our charter settled that nobody owed a game attendance simply because someone else loved it.
I signed last and discovered the portrait line had not secretly improved.
Shawna kissed my cheek. 'Congratulations, baby. Peace is official.'
'And expensive.' 'That part was official when you ordered the frame.'

games.burden: Repeated tending, expansion, currencies, waiting and item menus can become a workload. Movement and camera handling need a direct check. Online farm permissions matter when sharing; the source does not establish every activity as untimed or hold-free. This card covers the first game, not its sequel.

games.ruling: Return to the shared farm if its ongoing tasks remain pleasant. The coalition is signed, participation stays voluntary, and the portrait's continuing existence does not create collective financial responsibility.

games.case_title: The Village Had Enough Room for a Dance
scene: Staxel's shared village made Mika place the last two figures inside the miniature hotel. Rae and Nia stood on its little dance floor. My figure remained near the loading dock.
'A strong logistical role,' I said. 'A safe distance from the music controls,' Kit replied.
The signed agreement lay beneath the lamp. June and Dez had chosen different songs. Both selections would play. June's jacket waited over Dez's arm, borrowed again by asking.
The game's building and first-person controls still needed an actual trial. Our constructed room had already passed a simpler test: people could see, sit, leave and find each other.
Mercedes began the chosen music. Nia held out her hand to Rae. Rae took it without requesting another furniture inspection.
I offered Shawna my own hand. 'No introduction?' she asked. 'I'm trying a local custom.'
She came close. Velvet laughed beside the stage, Remy finally played the right fanfare, and nobody looked toward my portrait for permission.
Nigga, the place had become ours without becoming mine.

interludes.title: Peace Could Not Be Purchased with My Portrait Budget
paragraphs: The disagreement started with a line on the hotel's final service sheet: HOST TO DETERMINE PARTICIPANT SUITABILITY. I thought it meant deciding who could fit into Remy's spare crown.
Nia read it again. Rae put down her water.
'Suitable for what?' Rae asked.
The floor manager said it was standard wording. Nigga, people kept presenting standard as though it meant nobody had chosen it.
Kit asked whether it gave the door staff discretion to stop a guest who looked difficult. The manager said they would use judgment.
'Whose?' June asked.
I began saying the hotel was very welcoming. Shawna touched my sleeve. 'Let them answer.'
The manager explained that the host could approve the guest list. I was the host. Suddenly the expensive room had handed me a power I had been enjoying without examining its edges.

Rae said a security guard had asked her twice that afternoon whether she was working here. The second time, she was carrying her own coffee. Kit had walked beside her with a lighting cable and received a welcome.
'I told him she was with us,' Kit said.
Rae looked at her. 'I was already with myself.'
Kit nodded, embarrassed. 'I know. That's what came out.'
'It helped him stop asking. It also made you the person who could confirm I belonged.'
The manager said the guard was only checking. Velvet asked why checking had required the same person twice.
I recognised the expression on the manager's face. It was the one I used when I wanted a complaint to become a misunderstanding before anybody priced the remedy.
Nia did not translate Rae's sentence into nicer language. She asked the manager to answer it.
He could not explain the difference in treatment. He said he would speak to the guard.

Rae asked what would happen if it happened again while everybody was busy watching the stage. The manager gave his own name and said he would stay on the floor. Mika wrote down the number he supplied and checked that the phone rang.
A small test. No fanfare. A real person expected to answer.
Kit said she would correct her own introduction if it happened again. 'I don't need to tell him you're with me. I need to tell him he's already been answered.'
'And when I'm not standing there,' Rae said.
'Yes.'
The manager took the sheet away to replace the vague line. I watched him go, wondering why it had seemed so harmless until somebody described being on its receiving end.
June set her cup down. 'Your invitation put us on opposite sides before we got through the door. Then your hotel decided who looked like staff.'
I said the war title was a joke.
'I laughed,' she replied. 'I'm still asking you something.'

That stopped me more effectively than anger would have. I knew how to posture against an accusation. I had less practice staying still inside a question asked by someone who did not need to dislike me.
Rae touched the edge of the table she had repaired. 'I like making things work. I don't want that to become the price of being the kind of woman I am in this room.'
Kit said she recognised the temptation to earn welcome through competence. Then she stopped herself.
'That's my experience,' she said. 'It doesn't finish yours.'
Rae nodded. The distinction did not turn either of them into an enemy.

June tapped the portrait crate, where my folded war banner now lived. 'And I remain a Black butch whether your campaign knows where to put me or not. Don't use me as the exception that excuses the arrangement.'
'I won't,' I said.

She waited. I checked the entrance myself. The new signs named the rooms and where to ask for help. The banner stayed in its crate. The main title could remain the title of our absurd story without becoming sorting instructions for arriving guests.
Dez watched me straighten a sign. 'Careful with the corner. That's how jackets start wars.'
The laugh helped. It did not return the conversation to where it had been.

Mika brought the remaining staff costs. The performers had been paid, but the technicians' booked finish time came before the extra photographs I had requested. Someone would be packing down while I pretended the room existed indefinitely.
I offered the portrait's lighting budget.
'That money is already spent,' Nia said.
'A symbolic transfer.'
'The technician takes actual money,' Velvet replied.

Remy asked to cut his second entrance so the work could end on time. Velvet refused to solve my extension by making his performance smaller. Kit offered to shorten her own song, then admitted she did not really want to.
Nobody applauded her sacrifice. She looked relieved.
Rosa said the people clearing plates also had homes to reach. Tank moved the empty trays onto the trolley instead of describing his solidarity with the catering profession.
I asked the manager for the real cost of the time I had added. He returned with a number. It was less than the frame around my face.
Nigga, the comparison did something unpleasant to my priorities.
I paid the extension. We also ended the extra photo session early. Money bought the agreed work; it did not make staying late everyone's natural obligation.
Nia put the corrected sheet beside the game-night charter. 'These are arrangements for tonight. They don't buy forgiveness, desire or a story in which everybody now understands everybody.'

Mika put the remaining voluntary contributions on the table. The money had been collected for microphones and getting people home. I suggested applying it to the hotel's final total. Velvet asked which contributors had agreed to buy my decorations.
Kit pushed the envelope back toward Mika. 'I put in what I could. That doesn't buy me a better chair, and it doesn't become somebody else's portrait because the cheque was small.'

Rae proposed checking each remaining expense with Kit against the stated purposes. Mika would keep the record visible to contributors. Anything left would go back by the arrangement they had actually accepted. No surprise donation to my face.
I accepted that. The envelope stayed on their side of the table. Nigga, shared money had developed a location outside my pocket.
'Do they buy my dance?' I asked Shawna, attempting a recovery.
'No. I happen to want you. Don't make it accounting.'

Rae smiled at Nia. Nia smiled back, then turned toward the room. 'I also don't want our dance used as proof that the summit worked. I asked a woman I like to dance. That gets to be smaller than your campaign.'
I nodded. Porsche removed the planned photograph from the list without asking Nia to defend it.

Porsche asked what should happen if a recording continued after somebody said stop. Rae wanted it stopped, not debated over her head. Kit wanted a named person to take the request so the person objecting did not have to chase the whole room.

Mika took that job for the event. The photographer agreed to check a shot before using it and to set disputed material aside. If the plan broke, the recording would pause while the people involved decided the next step. An apology would not substitute for stopping the camera.
Nia approved the arrangement and declined the job of supervising it. She had a dance to attend. Porsche lowered her phone to show she had heard.

Remy sat on the arm of a chair. 'When people argue about whether men belong in a room, I hear the word differently from the way I did before transition. I still want friendships with women. I don't want my being a man treated as either a betrayal or a useful exception.'
June asked what he wanted tonight.
'My name used correctly. My number heard. My terrible fanfare tolerated once.'
'Once is a strong negotiating position,' Dez said.
Velvet flicked his crown with one finger. 'He is still responsible for the pun. Coalition will not save him.'
I liked that. Responsibility could remain particular. Nobody had to defend an entire category before admitting one man's joke was bad.

Kit asked whether our agreement should include never offending each other. Rae said no. She wanted people to stop, listen and repair what they could when they did. She did not promise to become instantly comfortable because the apology sounded polished.
Kit accepted that without asking how long Rae's patience would last.

The corrected service sheet returned. Nia read it; Mika checked the contact details; Rae said it answered the practical question she had asked. June asked whether everybody could still decline a game without being asked to explain their mood.
That line was already there. We kept it.
Dez reached for the jacket on her chair. 'And can we finally settle the sleeve business?'
Dez said she would return the coat when they signed. Could she then borrow it for the walk downstairs? June said yes.
Fifty-nine years of comedy briefly reduced itself to a question that could have been asked over a jukebox. Neither woman looked diminished by the answer.
I looked at the portrait crate. No communal payment, no title granting me the last word, no proof that I had become a better man merely because the floor was expensive.
Shawna took my hand anyway.
'You staying?' I asked.
'For the signing. For the dance. For you, if you stop trying to invoice the feeling.'
I kissed her hand, paid the remaining real workers and helped Mika clear the path to the table.
Peace was not everybody agreeing that I meant well.
Tonight, it was a door that stayed open, a number somebody would answer, work somebody would pay for, and enough room for two women to choose a song without becoming my evidence.

ending.title: Everybody Chose a Song; Nobody Bought My Face
paragraphs: The signatures were real. June wrote slowly, Dez added hers with a seamstress's steady care, and Nia's name crossed the line like an adventurous bird. Rae recognised it and signed beside it. The others followed in an order nobody would need to defend for sixty years.
Dez unfolded the old rental invoice while Nia checked the new names. June pointed at her own 1967 signature. Dez turned the paper over. Hers was on the back.
Both women stared. 'You signed the wrong side,' June said. 'You read the wrong side,' Dez replied. Nigga, I had hired a convention floor to resolve a failure to turn over one sheet.
I signed last. The portrait still received no reimbursement.
'Perhaps a commemorative allowance,' I murmured.
Shawna took the pen from my hand. 'Perhaps enjoy your wife.'
Nigga, finally a motion I could support without amendment.

The agreement protected an ordinary evening. Choose a game, ask for help, watch or decline. Stop when you want. Share the actual controls by agreement. Let different interests occupy the same room without drafting a winner.
Dez returned the jacket to June, then asked to borrow it for the walk downstairs. June said yes, provided it came back before another jukebox became obsolete.
'You make me sound unreliable,' Dez said.
'Only with sleeves,' June replied.
They laughed. The Blue Comet war ended without anyone fixing the weather in the official account.
June's chosen jukebox song played first. Dez tapped the table, pretending she had not liked it since 1967. Her own choice followed, and June sang the chorus incorrectly with magnificent commitment.
Then Mercedes began the song Rae and Nia had chosen.

Nia put her pen down and held out her hand. Rae took it and stood. No further invitation. No scheduling language. They walked onto the floor as two women who had spent the evening finding each other interesting and now wanted to be close.
Nia counted one step, caught Rae smiling and stopped counting aloud. Rae laughed softly. Nia drew a little nearer. Their first turn was imperfect and entirely theirs.
I signalled the photographer out of habit. Porsche touched his arm before he moved. Rae glanced over, shook her head once, and the camera stayed down.
Shawna took both my hands. 'Your turn.'
'For the photograph?'
'For me, nigga.'
I followed her onto the floor. The giant portrait watched from above, useful at last because it could not interrupt.

Velvet finished her number to the applause it deserved. Remy's fanfare arrived at the right moment and still contained the terrible pun. Kit sang. Rosa leaned against Tank; Dre collected the casserole dish only after checking nobody wanted more.
Mika placed the model hotel beside the signed agreement. Its little door remained open.

Later, Dez draped half the borrowed jacket across June's shoulders while they waited for the lift. June pretended the division needed measuring. Dez pulled her closer and said the seam allowance was generous.
The hotel manager handed me the portrait transport charge.
I looked at Shawna. She looked back with no intention of rescuing my budget and every intention of staying beside me.
I paid it.
Then I folded the receipt, put it in my own pocket and returned to the woman holding out her hand. Peace had its own music. For once, I did not need to introduce the singer.
